004: You got the pay rise. So why do you still feel broke? It catches almost everyone. It is called lifestyle creep. As you earn more, your spending quietly rises to match it. First it is a nicer phone. Then a bigger car, better nights out, and more subscriptions. Picture take home pay going from two thousand pounds a month to two thousand three hundred pounds. If spending climbs by the same three hundred pounds you are not one penny better off. But keep just half of that rise, and that is one hundred and fifty pounds a month, or one thousand eight hundred pounds a year, before any interest. Enjoying your money is not the problem. A better life is the whole point. The trouble is when the upgrades happen by accident. So next time you earn more, decide where the extra goes before it arrives. Some for today, and some for your future self. What is the first thing you upgraded when you started earning more? Tell me in the comments.
005: If budgeting feels confusing, try splitting your pay into just three pots. It takes about a minute, and it is the simplest budget there is. Half goes on needs, thirty percent on wants, and twenty percent on savings and paying off debt. Needs are the things you cannot skip, like rent, bills, food and getting to work. Wants are the nice things, like takeaways, subscriptions and nights out. On two thousand pounds of take home pay, that is one thousand pounds for needs, six hundred pounds for wants, and four hundred pounds to save or clear debt. If you live somewhere with high rent, needs might take far more than half. That is normal, so adjust the split to fit your life. The point is not being perfect. It is knowing where your money goes. Track one month, then decide what to change. What takes up most of your pay right now? Tell me in the comments.
006: You are waiting to feel ready. Here is the problem. Most people never do. Motivation is a feeling, and it is unreliable. Feelings come and go. It shows up on a good Monday, and it is gone by Wednesday. Discipline is different. It means doing the thing because you said you would, whether you feel like it or not. And here is what surprises people. Action usually comes first, and the motivation follows it. So make the first step tiny. Put your gym shoes by the door. Open the document. Read one page. Starting is the hard part. Then do it even on the bad days, even if it is only a smaller version. A rubbish workout still counts. It keeps the promise alive. Each kept promise teaches you that you can trust yourself. That trust is worth more than any burst of motivation. What have you been waiting to feel ready for? Tell me in the comments.
007: A share is not just a number on a screen. It is a tiny piece of a real business. Say a company splits itself into one million shares. If you own one hundred of them, you own one hundredth of one percent of the whole thing. Owning shares can come with a few rights. You may get a vote at the annual meeting, and a slice of any dividends the company pays out. There is no promise of either. Dividends can be cut, and many companies do not pay them at all. The share price is simply what buyers and sellers agree right now. It can move for many reasons, even when the business has not changed. If a company goes bust, shareholders are last in the queue, and they can lose everything they put in. So when you look at a share, try looking at the business behind it. This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. Before today, how did you think shares worked? Tell me in the comments.
008: Giving up coffee will not make you rich. Here is the thing that could help far more. Cut a three pounds coffee every working day, and you might save about seven hundred and fifty pounds a year. That is useful, but there is a limit to how much you can cut. Now earn just two pounds more an hour on a thirty seven and a half hour week. That is three thousand nine hundred pounds a year before tax, and there is no real ceiling. That is why your skills are your first asset. They go with you to every job, and nobody can take them away. The ones that travel furthest are simple. Selling, writing clearly, managing people, working with data, and using new tools. Just thirty minutes a day is over one hundred and eighty hours a year. That is enough to get seriously useful at something. Saving still matters. But when you have little to save, growing what you can earn may be the bigger lever. What skill are you learning right now? Tell me in the comments.
009: Think about the five people you spend the most time with. Your future might look a lot like theirs. It is not magic. We copy the people around us without noticing. Their habits, their standards, and what they think is normal. If everyone around you spends every penny, moans about work, and laughs at people trying to improve, that starts to feel like life. But if your friends read, train, save and build things, you start to raise your own bar, often without trying. That does not mean dropping old friends the moment you change. Loyalty matters, and good people can be at different stages. It means choosing where your time goes. Spend a little less with people who drain you, and a little more with those who lift you. And if you cannot find those people yet, books, clubs, courses and the gym are full of them. Then become that person for someone else. Who in your life pushes you to be better? Tell me in the comments.
010: Before you invest a single pound, you might need this first. It is the most boring money you will ever own, and maybe the most useful. An emergency fund is cash set aside for surprises, like a broken boiler, a car repair or losing your job. A common guideline is three to six months of your essential spending. Not your whole lifestyle, only the things you cannot skip. If your essentials cost one thousand five hundred pounds a month, that means somewhere between four thousand five hundred pounds and nine thousand pounds. That sounds like a lot, so build it in steps. Start by aiming for one month, then keep going from there. Without a buffer, one surprise bill can end up on a credit card, charging high interest for years. The right amount depends on your job security, who relies on you, and how you live. How many months could you cover today? Tell me in the comments.
011: Do you know how Apple really makes its money? In the twelve months to June twenty twenty six, Apple brought in about four hundred and sixty seven billion dollars. That is revenue, not profit. Around fifty three percent of that came from the iPhone. Around twenty six percent came from services, like the App Store, iCloud, Apple Music and payments. The bull case. Services bring repeat income from people who already own the devices, and those people often stay in the Apple world for years. The bear case. Over half of sales still depend on one product, and regulators in several countries are pressing on App Store rules. Rising memory costs can also squeeze margins. So a famous brand does not tell you whether a share is good value. That depends on the price, and the risks too. This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. Would you invest in a company like this? What would you watch? Let me know down in the comments.
012: In a famous experiment, children were offered one marshmallow now, or two if they could wait. Later studies found that background and home life explained much of the result. So it was never just about willpower. But the question is still a great one for adults. What am I giving up later to feel good right now? You face it all the time. The takeaway or the savings goal. Scrolling or sleep. Starting something new, or finishing what you started. And here is the useful bit. Waiting gets easier when you change your surroundings, not when you try to be stronger. Put your phone in another room. Delete the shopping app. Wait twenty four hours before buying anything you do not need. Nobody needs to wait for everything. Enjoy your life. Just make sure today is not stealing from the person you want to be. What is one thing you are waiting for right now? Tell me in the comments.
013: A one percent fee sounds tiny. Over thirty years, it might cost you thousands of pounds. Imagine investing ten thousand pounds once, and leaving it alone for thirty years. Assume it grows six percent a year after fees, compounding once a year. After thirty years, that is about fifty seven thousand four hundred pounds. Now add an extra one percent yearly fee, so it grows five percent instead. You end up with about forty three thousand two hundred pounds. That small difference costs you over fourteen thousand pounds and that is because fees compound too, just like your growth does. So it is worth checking the total yearly charges, including platform and fund fees. These can be easy to miss. Lower cost does not mean lower risk, though. Fees are just one part of the picture, and investments can always fall. Do you know what fees you pay on your savings or investments? Tell me in the comments.
014: You are comparing your chapter one to someone else's chapter twenty. And it is making you miserable. Social media only shows you the highlights. The car, the holiday, and the big announcement. You never see the debt, the doubt or the ten years before it. You are judging your behind the scenes against their best moments. Nobody wins that game, including them. And there is always somebody further ahead. If you measure yourself against the top, you can never arrive. So change who you compare yourself with. Look at who you were one year ago. Are you stronger, wiser, calmer, or better with money? And use envy as information. If someone's life makes you jealous, ask what part you actually want. Then take one small step towards it. And if a certain account always makes you feel worse, you are allowed to mute it. Protect your head. Who do you catch yourself comparing yourself to? Tell me in the comments.
015: Most people save whatever is left at the end of the month. Usually, that is nothing. Paying yourself first flips it around. You move money into savings the very day you get paid, before you can spend it. You can set up a standing order for payday, so saving happens automatically. You never have to think about it again. Even fifty pounds a month adds up to six hundred pounds a year, before any interest. It might not feel like much, but it is a start. Once it is automatic, you stop relying on willpower, and you simply learn to live on the rest. When you get a pay rise, some people raise their saving at the same time. That way, it never feels like you lost anything. But keep your essential bills covered first. Saving should never mean missing rent or going into debt. Do you save first, or at the end of the month? Tell me in the comments.
016: Most people spend more time choosing a new phone than researching a share. Here is one simple way to look at a company, in five steps. Step one. Understand the business. If you cannot explain how it makes money in one sentence, you are not ready yet. Step two. Look at the numbers. Is revenue growing? Is it making a profit? How much debt does it carry? Step three. Ask what protects it. A strong brand, loyal customers, or something rivals find hard to copy. Step four. Look at the price compared with its profits. A great company can still be priced for perfection. Step five. Write down what could go wrong. Then ask whether you could cope if the share fell by half. Doing the research does not remove the risk, and shares can still fall. This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. Do you pick single stocks or stick to index funds? Tell me in the comments.
017: One percent better does not feel like anything. And that is exactly why most people give up on it. Here is the maths. Multiply by one point zero one every day for a year, and you end up about thirty seven times where you started. Now flip it. Get just one percent worse each day, and you end up with almost nothing left. Real life is not that neat, of course. But the idea holds. Small things repeated beat big things done once. One page a day is around a dozen books a year. Ten minutes of walking, a small saving, or one honest conversation. It all stacks up. The hard part is that you will not see results for weeks. That is when most people quit, right before it starts to show. So do not judge a habit by this week. Judge it by whether you turned up. Your results come later, your identity starts now. What is one small thing you will do every day this month? Tell me in the comments.
018: Here is how eighty pounds can become one hundred pounds in your pension, and why so many young people have no idea it happens. When you pay into a pension, the government gives you back the income tax on that money. This is called tax relief. For a basic rate taxpayer, eighty pounds from your take home pay becomes one hundred pounds in the pension. The extra twenty pounds is tax relief at twenty percent. Higher rate taxpayers can usually claim more, sometimes through their tax return. How it works depends on your scheme. Some use relief at source, and others use net pay. So it is worth checking which one you are in. There are yearly limits, and the money is generally locked away until later in life. So a pension is not for short term goals. And pension investments can fall as well as rise, so what you get back is never guaranteed. Did you know about pension tax relief before today? Tell me in the comments.
019: Most side hustle videos are really selling you something. So here is the honest version. Passive income in a week is usually a fantasy. Nearly everything that pays takes real work first, often for months, before it pays anything. The most reliable starting point is simple. Sell a skill you already have. Tutoring, cleaning, design, repairs, editing or fitness. That is because you get paid from day one, there is little to buy, and you learn what people will actually pay for. Be careful with anything that asks you to pay first. Courses that promise easy money, and schemes where you need to recruit other people, are big red flags. And remember the tax. In the UK, you may need to tell the tax office once your side income goes over the one thousand pounds trading allowance. Start with one thing. Do it long enough to get good. Most people quit too soon, then blame the hustle. What side hustle have you tried? Did it make money? Tell me in the comments.
020: Every time you say yes to something, you are saying no to something else. Most of us never think about what. Yes to the extra shift can be no to your family. Yes to the night out can be no to the early gym session. And it costs money too. The hen do you cannot afford, or the loan to a mate that you will never see again. Often we say yes because we are scared of disappointing somebody. But if you always say yes, your own goals come last. The good news is that no does not need to be rude. Try, thanks for asking, but I cannot this time. Or, let me check and come back to you. You do not need a long excuse either. A short, kind answer is enough, and most people accept it far faster than you expect. Say yes to the things that matter. Saying no to the rest is how you make the room for them. What do you need to say no to this week? Tell me in the comments.
021: Look at how little Tesco keeps from every pound. In the first half of this financial year, Tesco reported retail sales of about thirty three point eight billion pounds. Most of that comes from selling food in the UK. Adjusted operating profit was about one point eight billion pounds. That works out to only around five pence for every pound of sales. Tesco's dividend yield was forecast at about three point four percent. Its net debt was about ten billion pounds, and dividends are never guaranteed. The bull case. People always need food, Clubcard keeps shoppers coming back, and Tesco raised the bottom of its profit guidance in October. The bear case. Margins are thin, discount rivals are fierce, and the shares were valued above their ten year average. A business you see every day can still be hard to value. This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. Would you invest in a company like this? What would you watch? Let me know down in the comments.
022: You do not have one credit score. You have several, and you can check them for free. A lot of people have never looked at theirs. It takes a few minutes. In the UK, lenders use reports from three main credit reference agencies. Each one may show something a little different. One. Register on the electoral roll at your address. It helps lenders confirm who you are. Two. Pay every bill on time. Missed payments can stay on your file for six years. Three. Try to keep card balances well below your limit. Four. Avoid lots of credit applications close together. Five. Having no history at all can count against you too, so a blank file is not always a good thing. Then check your reports for mistakes. An error can cost you a better deal. You have the right to ask for errors to be corrected. Have you ever checked your credit report? Tell me in the comments.
023: You will fail at something this year. What you do in the next forty eight hours matters far more than the failure. First, let it hurt. You do not have to pretend it is fine. Being gutted means that you actually cared. Nobody gets through life without this. Second, separate what happened from who you are. I failed the exam is very different from I am a failure. Third, get honest with three questions. What was in my control? What would I change? And what did this teach me? Fourth, take one small action straight away. Send the email. Book the resit. Make the call. Movement is what breaks the spell. And talk to someone. Keeping it all to yourself makes it heavier than it is. Most people who have done well have failed plenty. You can lose the job, the money or the game, and still come back from it. What setback taught you the most? Tell me in the comments.
024: Waiting ten years to start investing could cost you over a quarter of a million pounds. Here is how the sums work. Meet two people. Both invest two hundred pounds a month until they turn sixty five. Person A starts at twenty five. Person B waits, and starts at thirty five. Assume seven percent a year average growth, compounding monthly, with no fees and no adjustment for inflation. Person A ends up with about five hundred and twenty five thousand pounds. Person B gets about two hundred and forty four thousand pounds. Person A only paid in twenty four thousand pounds more, but ended up with more than double. Those extra ten years gave compounding more time to work, and the earlier start did most of the heavy lifting. Returns are not guaranteed, and they can be negative. What age did you start saving or investing? Tell me in the comments.
025: A share price of one hundred pounds tells you almost nothing. A ten pounds share could be far more expensive. Here is why. The P E ratio compares the price of a share with the profit behind it. P E means price to earnings. Say a share costs one hundred pounds and the company earns five pounds a year per share. one hundred pounds divided by five pounds is a P E of twenty. That means investors are paying twenty pounds for every one pound of yearly profit today. A high P E can mean people expect strong growth, or it can mean the share is priced too hopefully. A low P E can mean real value, or real trouble ahead. That is why it works best when you compare similar companies, in the same industry, and it means little when there are no profits. It is one clue, not an answer, and it does not tell you what a share will do next. This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. Had you heard of the P E ratio before today? Tell me in the comments.
026: Check your screen time. Three hours a day sounds normal. But do the maths on that. Three hours a day is over one thousand hours a year. That is around forty five full days, gone, with you awake for all of it. Imagine what forty five days could do. A new skill. A business started. A serious level of fitness. Time with the people you love. It is not because you are weak. These apps are built by very clever people to keep you watching. Willpower alone is a bad plan. So change the setup. Turn off the notifications. Keep your phone out of the bedroom. Move your apps off the home screen. You do not need to throw it away. Even cutting one hour a day gets you back more than two weeks a year. Yes, I know you are watching this on your phone. Use it on purpose, then put it down. What is your screen time right now? Be honest, and tell me in the comments.
027: A scammer can copy the name, the website and the paperwork of a real, regulated investment firm. These are called clone firms. They look completely genuine, and they catch out careful, smart people, not just the unlucky. Watch for the red flags. Guaranteed high returns. Pressure to act fast. And contact you never asked for. Be extra careful with offers on social media or messaging apps, and with anything involving crypto. Check the F C A register, then contact the firm using the details on the register, not the ones in the message. If you think you have been scammed, call your bank on one five nine, and report it to Report Fraud. Do it quickly, and try not to feel ashamed. If it sounds too good to be true, it usually is. Pass this on to someone who needs it. Have you or someone you know been targeted by a scam? Tell me in the comments.
028: In the UK, you can earn interest and investment growth completely tax free. Here is how that works. An ISA, or individual savings account, is a wrapper. It is not an investment by itself. It is the box you put your money in. Each tax year, from April sixth to April fifth, adults can put up to twenty thousand pounds into ISAs. Inside the wrapper, interest, dividends and growth are free from UK income tax and capital gains tax. There are a few main types. Cash ISAs, stocks and shares ISAs, Lifetime ISAs, and innovative finance ISAs. The allowance does not roll over. Any part you do not use is lost when the tax year ends. It starts again the next April. A stocks and shares ISA can still fall in value. The wrapper protects you from tax, not from losses, and tax rules can change. Do you have an ISA yet? Tell me in the comments.
029: Nobody who made it did it alone. So why are you trying to? A lot of us grow up believing that asking for help is weak. So we waste years learning the hard way, things that someone could teach us in an hour. Here is what most people do not realise. People generally like being asked. It feels good to be useful, and to be seen as someone who knows things. The trick is to make it easy to say yes. Be specific. Say, could I ask you two questions about how you got started? Not, can you be my mentor? Then actually use what they told you, and go back to tell them how it went. Hardly anybody does that, and people remember those who do. And ask for help before you are drowning. Whether it is money, work or your head, the earlier you speak up, the easier it is to fix. Then, when you are further along, turn around and help the next person. Who has helped you the most so far? Tell me in the comments.
030: Rolls-Royce does not make the cars. So what does it actually sell? Three main parts. Civil aerospace, which makes jet engines. Defence. And power systems, for data centres and ships. And here is the clever part. It earns a lot after selling the engine, because airlines pay for servicing based on how much those engines fly. In the first half of twenty twenty six, underlying revenue was about eleven point three billion pounds. Underlying operating profit was about two point five billion pounds, a margin of twenty two point five percent, and the company raised its full year guidance. The bull case. Engines bring in years of service income, and defence and power demand have been strong. The bear case. Flying can drop in a downturn, supply chain costs are high, and it warned about the conflict in the Middle East. This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. Would you invest in a company like this? What would you watch? Let me know down in the comments.
031: There are three ways to earn money. And only one of them can keep paying when you stop working. One, the employee. You rent out your time to someone else, for a set price. It is stable, with sick pay and a pension. Two, the freelancer. You still sell your time, but you set the price and choose the clients. You earn more per hour, and you have no cover when you stop. Three, the owner. You build something that can earn without you being there. A business with staff or systems, or a product that sells over and over. It comes with the most risk. Many new businesses fail, and owners often earn nothing for a long time. And you do not have to pick just one. Plenty of people keep the stable job, and build something on the side, in the evenings. The point is to know what you are selling. And to ask whether your hours could one day be working for you. Which one are you right now, and which one do you want to be? Tell me in the comments.
032: Confident people are not born that way. They have just collected more evidence. You cannot think your way into confidence. Staring in the mirror and telling yourself you are amazing will not do much, if deep down you do not believe it. Real confidence comes from doing a hard thing, and seeing that you survived it. Then your brain has proof. So the order is backwards from what most people think. It goes action first, and confidence after. You will feel scared first, every time. Start small. Speak up once in a meeting. Say hello to a stranger. Post the thing. Ask for what you want. Then pick something slightly harder. And you will mess some of it up. That is fine. That counts as evidence too, because you found out that you could get through it. In a year's time, you could look back and hardly recognise the person who was afraid of these things. What is one thing you will do this week that scares you? Tell me in the comments.
